title: Design a Live Streaming Platform
summary: Sub-second-latency ingest-to-viewer pipeline for content that doesn't exist until the moment it's watched — the opposite of VOD's precompute-then-serve model.

slides.markdown:
The prompt: a streamer broadcasts live, and thousands of viewers watch with minimal delay behind the live moment.

[design-video-streaming-platform](design-video-streaming-platform) can precompute a rendition ladder before anyone watches, because the video already exists. Live content doesn't exist until the instant it's captured — every rendition has to be produced and distributed in real time, which inverts nearly every assumption that made VOD's design tractable.

**Functional:** ingest a live broadcast, transcode it in real time, distribute it to viewers, and support live chat alongside the video.

**Non-functional:** a hard **end-to-end latency budget** (seconds, not the tens-of-seconds some platforms tolerate — the gap directly affects how "live" a live chat reaction feels), tolerance for **concurrent viewer spikes** when a stream suddenly gets popular mid-broadcast, and a chat system that scales independently of video delivery.

slides.sectionTitle: Back-of-envelope: ingest bitrate, fan-out, and total egress during a spike
slides.markdown:
One streamer ingests at, say, 6Mbps. That single ingest stream might fan out to 100,000 concurrent viewers at an average 3Mbps each (mixed renditions) — **300Gbps of egress from one broadcast**, compared to 6Mbps of ingest. The fan-out ratio, not the ingest bitrate, is what dominates capacity planning.

A single breakout stream spiking from 1,000 to 100,000 viewers in minutes (a moment going viral) means egress capacity has to be provisioned — or elastically available — far ahead of steady-state need, since there's no equivalent of pre-caching for content that doesn't exist yet.

`startStream()` provisions an ingest endpoint and stream key for the broadcaster's encoder to push to (commonly RTMP or SRT). Viewers fetch a **playback manifest** — but unlike VOD, this manifest is a living document that grows a new segment reference every couple of seconds as the broadcast continues, rather than listing a complete, fixed set upfront.

That continuously-updating manifest is the core API difference from VOD: the client keeps re-polling or receiving pushed updates to discover newly available segments, since the full list can never be known in advance for something still happening.

slides.sectionTitle: Live transcoding: producing renditions in real time
slides.markdown:
Live transcoding takes the incoming stream and produces the same kind of rendition ladder VOD does (multiple resolutions/bitrates) — but continuously, a few seconds behind real time, instead of once ahead of any viewing. Every rendition has to be produced *before* the first viewer can request it, so transcode speed directly adds to end-to-end latency, unlike VOD where transcode time only affects publish delay.

This is why live transcoding is usually run on dedicated, latency-optimized hardware (hardware encoders, GPU-accelerated pipelines) rather than the batch-oriented worker pools that suffice for VOD.

![Ingest-to-viewer pipeline with per-hop latency budget](assets/live-ingest-pipeline.svg)

Each hop adds latency that VOD doesn't have to worry about paying at view time, since VOD already finished transcoding long before anyone watches — here, the sum of every hop's delay is what a viewer experiences as "how far behind live am I."

assets.alt: Ingest-to-viewer pipeline with per-hop latency budget

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: small low-latency segments vs VOD's larger chunks
slides.markdown:
| | Live (low-latency) segments | VOD segments |
|---|---|---|
| Typical segment length | ~1-2 seconds, sometimes sub-second (chunked transfer) | ~6-10 seconds |
| Reason for size | Every second of segment length adds directly to end-to-end latency | Larger segments reduce request overhead with no latency cost — the video already exists |
| Manifest behavior | Continuously appended as the broadcast continues | Complete and fixed once the video is published |
| Trade-off | Smaller segments mean more requests/overhead per second of video | Fewer requests, more efficient delivery, latency irrelevant |

**How to decide:** shrink segment size only as far as the latency budget requires — going smaller than necessary adds request overhead and CDN cache-churn without buying a latency improvement anyone notices.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: viewer fan-out during a spike
slides.markdown:
![Fan-out tree widening from one ingest stream to many edge nodes during a viewer spike](assets/live-fanout-spike.svg)

The fan-out tree, not the single ingest stream, is what has to scale elastically and fast — a popular stream's viewer count can grow far quicker than infrastructure can be manually provisioned, which is why this has to be automatic.

assets.alt: Fan-out tree widening from one ingest stream to many edge nodes during a viewer spike

slides.sectionTitle: The bottleneck: transcoding falling behind ingest under load
slides.markdown:
If the real-time transcode stage can't keep pace with the incoming stream — say a burst of simultaneous streams saturates the transcode fleet — segments get produced later than they should, and that lag directly adds to the latency every viewer experiences, or in the worst case causes the stream to visibly stutter or drop frames.

Unlike VOD's transcode backlog (which only delays publish, invisible to anyone not already trying to watch), a live transcode backlog is instantly visible to every current viewer simultaneously — there's no queue to hide it in, which is why live transcode capacity needs more aggressive headroom than VOD's.

A popular stream's chat can generate thousands of messages per minute across hundreds of thousands of viewers — far too much for every viewer to receive every message individually without a dedicated fan-out path, and it must run **independently** of video delivery so a chat surge never competes with video bandwidth or adds video latency.

Most platforms scale this with pub/sub fan-out per stream (one publish, many subscribed viewer connections) and apply rate limiting or sampling under extreme load — showing a representative subset of messages rather than literally every one to every viewer once volume passes what's readable anyway.

slides.sectionTitle: Trade-off: lower latency vs playback stability
slides.markdown:
A smaller client-side buffer gets a viewer closer to true live, but leaves less cushion to absorb network jitter — a brief bandwidth dip causes a visible stall. A larger buffer smooths over jitter but pushes the viewer further behind the live moment.

**How to decide:** tune buffer size to the use case — a few seconds of extra delay is invisible for most broadcasts, but unacceptable for anything with real-time interaction (a live auction, an interactive Q&A) where viewer reactions need to land close to the moment they're reacting to.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: applying the VOD precompute-then-cache model to live
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We already built a great VOD pipeline — live is just VOD where we publish sooner."

**Why it's wrong:** VOD's entire design leans on the video already existing, so transcoding and CDN pre-warming can happen ahead of any viewer request; live content doesn't exist until the moment it's captured, so every hop — transcode, distribution, cache warm — has to happen in the seconds between capture and playback, adding real minutes of delay if you reuse VOD's larger segments and batch-style transcode workers.

**Correct model:** treat live as a fundamentally different latency budget problem — small segments, real-time transcode capacity with aggressive headroom, and a fan-out path built to scale in seconds, not VOD's pipeline running faster.
